---
title: "Licence"
---


**AGPL-3.0-or-later**, the same terms as zotQDA, qdaZ and the Python twin
qdaPy. The full text ships with R, in `share/licenses/AGPL-3`.

## What you produce with qdaR is yours

Figures, data frames, coefficients, reports, the analysis scripts you wrote:
the licence places no condition on any of it. That is granted explicitly as an
additional permission under section 7 of the AGPL.

In this package the permission is part of `LICENSE`, because
`License: AGPL-3 + file LICENSE` in `DESCRIPTION` means *the AGPL plus what is
in that file*: that is where an R package states additional terms. The other
projects keep the same wording in a file called `LICENSE-EXCEPTION.md`.

Strictly speaking the clause changes nothing, a copyleft licence has never
reached into a program's output, and the Free Software Foundation says so in
its own FAQ. But the belief that it does is persistent enough to make an ethics
board or a university legal office hesitate, and a figure in a submitted
manuscript is not the place for a licensing question. So it is written down.

The permission also covers the fragments of the package that necessarily end up
inside your output: axis labels, caption wording, the default palette, column
names of returned data frames, message and warning texts.

## Commercial use does not need a commercial licence

This is the most common misunderstanding about the AGPL. You may use qdaR in a
company, in paid consulting, in contract research and in work you are paid for,
without asking anyone and without paying anything.

What the AGPL asks is that if you distribute a *modified version*, or let
others use one over a network, you pass the source on under the same terms.
That is the only condition, and it holds for everyone: qdaR is **not**
dual-licensed, and there is no proprietary exception to be bought.

## Contributions

Nothing to sign. There is no contributor licence agreement, because there is no
second licence that would need one. You contribute under the AGPL and keep your
copyright.
